title: Demonstrate a basic understanding of the physiological processes in plant growth and development

lessons.title: Photosynthesis, respiration and water relations
lessons.html:
Growth and development

Growth is an irreversible increase in size or mass. Development is the progression through life stages: germination, vegetative growth, flowering, fruiting, ripening and senescence. Both are driven by physiological processes that respond to the environment and to management.

Photosynthesis

In chloroplasts, light energy converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen. The rate depends on:

  • Light: more light increases photosynthesis up to a saturation point. Canopy management, row direction and pruning affect light interception.
  • Carbon dioxide: enters through stomata; closed stomata limit uptake.
  • Temperature: each crop has an optimum range; very high or low temperatures slow enzyme activity.
  • Water: water stress closes stomata.
  • Nutrients: nitrogen and magnesium are part of chlorophyll; deficiencies reduce green leaf area.

Plants differ: C4 plants such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane are more efficient in hot, bright conditions than C3 plants such as wheat, beans and most vegetables.

Respiration

Respiration breaks down sugars to release energy for growth and maintenance. It runs day and night and rises with temperature. Warm nights increase respiration losses, reducing net growth. After harvest, respiration continues and uses stored sugars, so produce is cooled to slow it.

Water relations and transpiration

Water moves from soil into roots, up the xylem and out of the stomata as vapour. Transpiration cools leaves and drives nutrient transport. When soil water runs low, plants close stomata, wilt and slow growth. Critical periods for water stress include germination, flowering and fruit or grain fill; stress then causes the biggest yield losses.

Translocation

Sugars move in the phloem from sources (mature leaves) to sinks (growing tips, roots, fruit, tubers). Management can shift the balance: fruit thinning reduces the number of sinks so each fruit gets more sugar; heavy vegetative growth can compete with fruit.

lessons.title: Plant hormones and developmental stages
lessons.html:
Plant hormones

Plant growth regulators are chemical messengers that control growth and development.

HormoneMain effectsPractical relevance
AuxinsCell elongation, apical dominance, root initiationRooting hormones for cuttings; topping removes auxin source and releases side buds
GibberellinsStem elongation, seed germination, fruit sizeUsed in some table grape and citrus programmes
CytokininsCell division, delay leaf ageing, side shoot growthTissue culture; some fruit size products
Abscisic acid (ABA)Stomatal closure under stress, seed and bud dormancyExplains drought responses and dormancy
EthyleneRipening, leaf and fruit drop, flower induction in some cropsRipening rooms for bananas and avocados; ethylene control in cold stores

Commercial growth regulators may only be used as registered and according to the label and the adviser's programme.

Environmental control of development

  • Photoperiod: day length triggers flowering in many plants. Short-day onions are suited to South African winter production; long-day cultivars are not.
  • Temperature and heat units: development speed is often predicted using growing degree days; maize maturity classes are based on heat units.
  • Vernalisation: some crops need cold to flower, such as winter wheat cultivars.
  • Chilling requirement: deciduous fruit trees need enough winter chill to break bud dormancy evenly; warm winters cause uneven budbreak.

Developmental stages and management

  1. Germination and emergence: needs moisture, oxygen and suitable soil temperature.
  2. Vegetative growth: leaf area builds; nitrogen and water are key.
  3. Flowering and pollination: sensitive to heat, frost and water stress; pollinators needed in many crops.
  4. Fruit set and fill: high demand for sugars, potassium and water.
  5. Ripening and maturity: controlled by hormones like ethylene; timing of harvest affects quality.
  6. Senescence: ageing and leaf drop.

Matching operations to stages improves results: fertilise when uptake is high, irrigate carefully at critical stages, protect flowers from frost.

Key points

  • Photosynthesis makes sugars; respiration uses them, day and night.
  • Water stress at flowering and fill causes the biggest yield losses.
  • Sugars move from sources to sinks; thinning shifts the balance.
  • Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ABA and ethylene control growth and development.
  • Day length, heat units, vernalisation and chilling govern developmental timing.
